Jabbok
JAB-uk
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Yabboq (H2999), a river (a tributary of the Jordan) east of the Jordan; the name resembles the Hebrew 'abaq ("to wrestle"), a wordplay with Jacob (Ya'aqob) and the wrestling that took place there.

See also: Jabbok

📖 Biblical Definition

The Jabbok was a river east of the Jordan, a tributary flowing into it, famous as the place where Jacob wrestled through the night with a mysterious man — God Himself in the form of a man — and was given the name Israel. On the night before his dreaded reunion with Esau, Jacob sent his family and possessions over the ford of the Jabbok and was left alone; "and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day" (Gen 32:24). The wordplay is deliberate in the Hebrew: at the Jabbok (Yabboq), Jacob (Ya'aqob) wrestled ('abaq). Jacob prevailed and would not let the man go until he blessed him; the man touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh, putting it out of joint, so that Jacob limped ever after; and he gave Jacob a new name: "Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed" (Gen 32:28). Jacob named the place Peniel ("the face of God"), saying, "I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved" (Gen 32:30). The Jabbok wrestling is one of the most profound passages in Scripture: the supplanter Jacob, who had spent his life grasping and scheming, is met by God, brought to the end of his own strength (his thigh disjointed), and transformed — clinging now not to win by craft but to receive a blessing he cannot earn. He prevails not by overpowering God but by holding on in desperate dependence, refusing to let go. He emerges with a new name, a new limp, and a new character. The Jabbok teaches that God's transforming encounter often comes in the night of our deepest fear, that He must sometimes cripple our self-reliance before He can bless us, and that the prevailing faith is the faith that, brought to the end of itself, clings to God and will not let Him go.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A river east of the Jordan where Jacob wrestled through the night with God in the form of a man, was crippled in the thigh, and was renamed Israel (Gen 32:24-30); the place (Peniel, "face of God") of God's transforming encounter that breaks self-reliance and gives the prevailing faith that clings to God.

JABBOK, proper noun. Hebrew Yabboq (H2999); a river east of the Jordan, a tributary flowing into it.

Where Jacob, alone the night before meeting Esau, wrestled with a man until daybreak (Gen 32:24).

Hebrew wordplay: at the Jabbok (Yabboq), Jacob (Ya'aqob) wrestled ('abaq).

The man (God in human form) disjointed Jacob's thigh and renamed him Israel, "for as a prince hast thou power with God" (Gen 32:28).

Jacob named the place Peniel, "the face of God" (Gen 32:30); the place of God's transforming, self-reliance-breaking encounter.

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 32:24 — "And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day."

Genesis 32:26 — "And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."

Genesis 32:28 — "And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed."

Hosea 12:4 — "Yea, he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him: he found him in Bethel, and there he spake with us."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Jabbok is corrupted when the wrestling is read as a mere legend or as Jacob overpowering God by strength, when the crippling is missed as God's gracious breaking of self-reliance, or when the prevailing is divorced from the desperate clinging dependence that defines it.

expand to see more

Overpowering-God misreading. The Jabbok wrestling can be misread as Jacob, by sheer strength or persistence, defeating God and forcing a blessing. The narrative says the opposite: the man "saw that he prevailed not against him" only because he chose not to exert His full power, and with a single touch He disjointed Jacob's thigh, instantly demonstrating who was stronger. Jacob "prevailed" not by overpowering God but by refusing to let go — by clinging in desperate dependence even when crippled and unable to fight: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me" (Gen 32:26). The prevailing faith is not the faith that overpowers God but the faith that, brought to the end of its own strength, holds on to Him and will not release its grip.

The Jabbok has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the pattern of God's transforming encounter: He meets His servant in the night of his deepest fear, brings him to the end of his self-reliance (the disjointed thigh, the lifelong limp), and there gives him a new name and a new character. Hosea reflects on it: Jacob "had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication" (Hos 12:4) — the prevailing was through weeping and supplication, not strength. God often must cripple our scheming self-confidence before He can bless us; the limp is the mark of the man who has met God and been changed.

A river east of the Jordan where Jacob wrestled with God in human form, was crippled, and renamed Israel (Gen 32:24-30); the place (Peniel) of God's transforming encounter that breaks self-reliance and gives the prevailing, clinging faith.
